```{python}
import pandas as pd

# This is the TEST-DATA deck — always reads the synthetic placeholder, never
# the live Google Sheet. See week3-live.qmd for the in-class version.
df = pd.read_csv("data/synthetic_reaction_times.csv")
# df = pd.read_csv("https://docs.google.com/spreadsheets/d/e/2PACX-1vRWIOZ03GpUJgqvGVmI9cih169mMq0ajLMj6a0VTd2tytB3K5BmX5AUiKQ8FKIL6KUKEcgb-1LR-1eM/pub?gid=0&single=true&output=csv")

if 'name' in df.columns and 'student_name' not in df.columns:
    df = df.rename(columns={'name': 'student_name'})
if 'caffeine' not in df.columns:
    df['caffeine'] = 'Unknown'
df['caffeine'] = df['caffeine'].fillna('Unknown')

# finger_mm may not exist on older submissions — coerce and tolerate absence
if 'finger_mm' not in df.columns:
    df['finger_mm'] = None
df['finger_mm'] = pd.to_numeric(df['finger_mm'], errors='coerce')

students = sorted(df['student_name'].unique().tolist())

# One row per student: mean reaction time, device, caffeine, finger length
student_summary = (
    df.groupby('student_name')
    .agg(mean_rt=('reaction_time_ms', 'mean'),
         device=('device', 'first'),
         caffeine=('caffeine', 'first'),
         finger_mm=('finger_mm', 'first'))
    .reset_index()
    .round(1)
)

# Joint device x caffeine counts, one row per student (not per trial)
students_df = df.drop_duplicates('student_name')
joint_table = (
    students_df.groupby(['device', 'caffeine']).size()
    .reset_index(name='count')
)

# NaN (e.g. missing finger_mm) is not valid JSON. All ojs_define() values share
# one JSON payload, so a single stray NaN anywhere breaks every variable in the
# call — clean each one before handing it over.
df_clean = df.astype(object).where(df.notna(), None)
student_summary_clean = student_summary.astype(object).where(student_summary.notna(), None)
joint_table_clean = joint_table.astype(object).where(joint_table.notna(), None)

ojs_define(
    data            = df_clean.to_dict(orient='records'),
    students        = students,
    student_summary = student_summary_clean.to_dict(orient='records'),
    joint_table     = joint_table_clean.to_dict(orient='records'),
)
```

```{python}
import numpy as np

# ── A second, separate illustrative dataset for the scatter / bin-scatter /
# log-transform teaching sequence ("Scatterplot and bin-scatter", "Does
# logging reaction time help?"). Deliberately NOT finger length -- students
# are set a task later to build exactly that scatter themselves, so the
# worked example here uses a different x (a plausible, separate driver of
# reaction time: hours of sleep the night before), generated to reliably
# show what logging is *for*. First version used a handful of moderately
# slow trials -- the resulting raw/log contrast was real but too subtle to
# read at a glance (R^2 improved only ~1.8x, main cluster still occupied
# ~60% of either axis). Rebuilt with a few *severe* "very bad day" outliers
# instead: the main cluster now occupies only ~22% of the raw axis (crushed
# by the outliers stretching it) vs ~39% of the log axis -- a genuinely
# visible difference in how much of the chart the actual pattern gets to
# use, not just a marginally-better R^2. Verified numerically before
# committing: skew 3.85, log-linear R^2 (~0.24) still roughly 2.4x the raw
# fit's (~0.10).
np.random.seed(21)
n_sleep = 66
sleep_hours = np.round(np.random.uniform(4, 9.5, n_sleep), 1)
_a, _b, _sigma = 5.95, 0.09, 0.075
_log_rt = _a - _b * sleep_hours + np.random.normal(0, _sigma, n_sleep)
sleep_rt = np.clip(np.exp(_log_rt), 150, None).round(1)

# A few severe "very bad day" trials -- the real-world reason reaction time
# has a long right tail, deliberately extreme here so the raw-vs-logged
# contrast is unmistakable rather than subtle
_rng = np.random.default_rng(5)
_n_out = 3
_idx_out = _rng.choice(n_sleep, _n_out, replace=False)
sleep_hours = np.concatenate([sleep_hours, sleep_hours[_idx_out]])
sleep_rt    = np.concatenate([sleep_rt, _rng.uniform(650, 900, _n_out).round(1)])

sleep_scatter_data = [
    {'sleep_hours': float(sleep_hours[i]), 'reaction_time_ms': float(sleep_rt[i])}
    for i in range(len(sleep_hours))
]

ojs_define(sleep_scatter_data = sleep_scatter_data)
```

## A shortcut for HR

::: {.instructions-box}
The reaction-time test works, but it takes ten trials per person to administer. HR wants something faster: **"find us a quick physical measurement that predicts reaction time, and we'll screen candidates on that instead."**
:::

::: {.fragment}
That's why we collected **index finger length** back in Week 1.

Is it a fast, reliable stand-in for the real test? Today gives us the tools to answer that properly — and the discipline not to answer it too quickly.
:::

---

## When y met x

---

## The y and the x

Much of data analysis is about comparing values of a **y** variable across values of an **x** variable — uncovering patterns of association.

- By convention, **y** is the variable we're interested in; **x** is what we compare across
- **Goal 1 — prediction:** use x to predict y, without needing to know *why*
- **Goal 2 — causal effect:** learn what would happen to y if we *changed* x

::: {.fragment}
HR's proxy-test idea is a **prediction** goal, dressed up as if it were free of that distinction. Keep watching for where the two goals get blurred.
:::

::: {style="font-size:0.75em;color:#999;margin-top:12px;"}
Source: Békés & Kézdi (2021), *Data Analysis for Business, Economics, and Policy*, Ch. 4
:::

---

## Conditional probability

---

## Conditioning on x

- **Comparison → conditioning.** Comparing y by values of x means we **condition** y on x
- x is the **conditioning variable**; y is the **outcome variable**
- **Conditional probability:** $P(A \mid B) = \dfrac{P(A \text{ and } B)}{P(B)}$
- **Joint probability:** $P(A \text{ and } B) = P(A) \times P(B)$ — *if A and B are independent*
- **Independence:** $P(A \mid B) = P(A)$ and $P(B \mid A) = P(B)$

::: {style="font-size:0.75em;color:#999;margin-top:12px;"}
Source: Békés & Kézdi (2021), Ch. 4
:::

## Device and caffeine: our own joint table

```{ojs}
{
  if (!joint_table.length) return html`<p style="color:#aaa;">Not enough data yet.</p>`
  const devices = [...new Set(joint_table.map(d => d.device))]
  const caffs = [...new Set(joint_table.map(d => d.caffeine))]
  const grandTotal = d3.sum(joint_table, d => d.count)
  const cell = (dev, caf) => joint_table.find(r => r.device === dev && r.caffeine === caf)?.count ?? 0
  const rowTotal = dev => d3.sum(caffs, c => cell(dev, c))
  const colTotal = caf => d3.sum(devices, d => cell(d, caf))

  return html`<table style="width:80%;margin:0 auto;border-collapse:collapse;font-family:sans-serif;font-size:0.95em;">
    <thead><tr style="background:#1a1a2e;color:white;">
      <th style="padding:10px 18px;text-align:left;">Device \\ Caffeine</th>
      ${caffs.map(c => `<th style="padding:10px 18px;text-align:right;">${c}</th>`).join('')}
      <th style="padding:10px 18px;text-align:right;background:#2d6a4f;">Total</th>
    </tr></thead>
    <tbody>
      ${devices.map((dev,i) => `<tr style="${i%2===1?'background:#fafafa;':''}border-bottom:1px solid #eee;">
        <td style="padding:9px 18px;font-weight:700;">${dev}</td>
        ${caffs.map(c => `<td style="padding:9px 18px;text-align:right;color:#457b9d;">${cell(dev,c)}</td>`).join('')}
        <td style="padding:9px 18px;text-align:right;font-weight:700;background:#f0f4f8;">${rowTotal(dev)}</td>
      </tr>`).join('')}
      <tr style="border-top:2px solid #1a1a2e;">
        <td style="padding:9px 18px;font-weight:700;background:#f0f4f8;">Total</td>
        ${caffs.map(c => `<td style="padding:9px 18px;text-align:right;font-weight:700;background:#f0f4f8;">${colTotal(c)}</td>`).join('')}
        <td style="padding:9px 18px;text-align:right;font-weight:700;background:#e9edf1;">${grandTotal}</td>
      </tr>
    </tbody>
  </table>`
}
```

::: {.fragment}
Row and column **totals** give you the marginals directly — no need to derive $P(\text{Device})$ or $P(\text{Caffeine})$ yourself before you can condition.
:::

## Task — condition on our own data

::: {.instructions-box}
On paper, using the table above: what is $P(\text{Caffeine} = \text{Yes} \mid \text{Device} = \text{Phone})$?

Does knowing someone's device change your guess about their caffeine use? How much would you trust that conclusion, given how many observations it's based on?
:::

::: {.fragment}
**Independence is not a yes/no question you can answer from a table this small.** Any real sample will show *some* numerical gap between the conditional and marginal probabilities, purely by chance — even when the true population relationship is independence. Telling a real pattern from sampling noise is exactly what Week 2's tools (standard errors, hypothesis tests) are for. With this few observations, "we can't tell yet" is the honest answer, not a verdict either way.
:::

## Visualising with a stacked bar chart

```{ojs}
stacked_data = {
  if (!joint_table.length) return []
  const devices = [...new Set(joint_table.map(d => d.device))]
  return devices.flatMap(dev => {
    const rows = joint_table.filter(d => d.device === dev)
    const tot = d3.sum(rows, d => d.count)
    return rows.map(r => ({ ...r, pct: r.count / tot }))
  })
}
```

```{ojs}
{
  if (!stacked_data.length) return html`<p style="color:#aaa;">Not enough data yet.</p>`
  return Plot.plot({
    height: 280,
    marginLeft: 60,
    x: { label: "Device" },
    y: { label: "% within device", percent: true },
    color: { legend: true, domain: ["Yes","No","Unknown"], range: ["#e63946","#457b9d","#ccc"] },
    marks: [
      Plot.barY(stacked_data, { x: "device", y: "pct", fill: "caffeine", order: "caffeine" }),
      Plot.ruleY([0]),
    ]
  })
}
```

::: {.fragment}
Stacked to 100% within each device — this shows $P(\text{Caffeine} \mid \text{Device})$ directly, not the raw counts.
:::

---

## Conditional distribution and expectation

---

## The conditional mean

The **conditional expectation** of y for a given value of x:

$$E[y \mid x]$$

- The mean of y, computed separately for each value (or group) of x
- With few x values, a histogram or box plot per group works well (Week 1)
- With **many** x values — like finger length in mm — group into **bins** first

::: {style="font-size:0.75em;color:#999;margin-top:12px;"}
Source: Békés & Kézdi (2021), Ch. 4
:::

## Task — compute the conditional mean, by hand

::: {.instructions-box}
Using the class's finger-length and reaction-time data: split students into three roughly equal-sized groups by finger length (short / medium / long), then compute the mean reaction time within each group. Compare to the chart on the next slide.
:::

## Binning finger length

```{ojs}
{
  const rows = student_summary.filter(d => d.finger_mm != null && !isNaN(d.finger_mm))
  if (rows.length < 3) {
    return html`<div class="instructions-box">Not enough finger-length data yet to bin — this will populate once more of the class has submitted through the updated tool.</div>`
  }
  const vals = rows.map(d => d.finger_mm).sort((a,b) => a-b)
  const q1 = d3.quantile(vals, 1/3), q2 = d3.quantile(vals, 2/3)
  const binOf = f => f <= q1 ? "Short" : f <= q2 ? "Medium" : "Long"
  const binned = rows.map(d => ({ ...d, bin: binOf(d.finger_mm) }))
  const grouped = ["Short","Medium","Long"].map(b => {
    const g = binned.filter(d => d.bin === b)
    return { bin: b, n: g.length, mean_rt: g.length ? d3.mean(g, d => d.mean_rt) : null }
  }).filter(g => g.n > 0)

  return Plot.plot({
    height: 300,
    marginLeft: 60,
    x: { label: "Finger length bin", domain: ["Short","Medium","Long"] },
    y: { label: "E[reaction time | bin] (ms)" },
    marks: [
      Plot.barY(grouped, { x: "bin", y: "mean_rt", fill: "#457b9d", fillOpacity: 0.8 }),
      Plot.text(grouped, { x: "bin", y: "mean_rt", text: d => `n=${d.n}`, dy: -10, fill: "#333", fontSize: 12 }),
      Plot.ruleY([0]),
    ]
  })
}
```

## Scatter, covariance, correlation

---

## Scatterplot and bin-scatter {.smaller}

A **scatterplot** puts two variables on two axes, one dot per observation. It's one of the most powerful ways to see whether a relationship exists between two variables — no formula required, just look.

::: {.fragment}
Not finger length this time — you'll build that scatter yourselves shortly. Here it's a separate illustrative case: **hours of sleep the night before**, against reaction time, for 69 trials.
:::

```{ojs}
{
  return Plot.plot({
    height: 300,
    marginLeft: 60,
    x: { label: "Sleep the night before (hours)" },
    y: { label: "Reaction time (ms)" },
    marks: [
      Plot.dot(sleep_scatter_data, { x: "sleep_hours", y: "reaction_time_ms", fill: "#457b9d", r: 5, fillOpacity: 0.75,
                       tip: true, title: d => `${d.sleep_hours}h sleep, ${d.reaction_time_ms}ms` }),
    ]
  })
}
```

::: {.fragment}
Every dot is one trial. There's a real pattern here, but a handful of slow "attention lapse" trials — everyone has them, however well-rested — stretch the top of the scale and make it hard to see. Often with more data this will struggle to fit on a scatter. In those cases, a **bin-scatter** can reveal the pattern without the clutter.
:::

## The bin-scatter

The **conditional mean per bin** — one dot per observed sleep value, not a wide bucket like "Short / Medium / Long" on the finger-length slide.

```{ojs}
{
  const grouped = d3.rollups(sleep_scatter_data, v => d3.mean(v, d => d.reaction_time_ms), d => d.sleep_hours)
    .map(([sleep_hours, mean_rt]) => ({ sleep_hours, mean_rt }))
    .sort((a, b) => a.sleep_hours - b.sleep_hours)

  return Plot.plot({
    height: 340,
    marginLeft: 60,
    x: { label: "Sleep the night before (hours)" },
    y: { label: "E[reaction time | sleep hours] (ms)" },
    marks: [
      Plot.dot(grouped, { x: "sleep_hours", y: "mean_rt", fill: "#2d6a4f", r: 5, fillOpacity: 0.85,
                       tip: true, title: d => `${d.sleep_hours}h: ${d.mean_rt.toFixed(0)}ms` }),
    ]
  })
}
```

::: {.fragment}
The lapses still show — a few bins still sit high — but the underlying downward trend reads far more clearly than in the raw scatter.
:::

## Does logging reaction time help? {.smaller}

Week 1 found reaction time is closer to log-normal than normal — a floor, no ceiling, long right tail. Gabor's own case study logs a skewed variable for exactly this reason: it stretches out the crowded end and compresses the tail, so a pattern against x is easier to read.

::: {.two-col}
::: {.col}
**Logged**

```{ojs}
{
  return Plot.plot({
    height: 340,
    marginLeft: 55,
    x: { label: "Sleep the night before (hours)" },
    y: { label: "ln(reaction time)" },
    marks: [
      Plot.dot(sleep_scatter_data, { x: "sleep_hours", y: d => Math.log(d.reaction_time_ms), fill: "#2d6a4f", r: 5, fillOpacity: 0.75,
                       tip: true, title: d => `${d.sleep_hours}h sleep, ${d.reaction_time_ms}ms` }),
    ]
  })
}
```
:::
::: {.col .fragment data-fragment-index="1"}
**Raw scale**

```{ojs}
{
  return Plot.plot({
    height: 340,
    marginLeft: 55,
    x: { label: "Sleep the night before (hours)" },
    y: { label: "Reaction time (ms)" },
    marks: [
      Plot.dot(sleep_scatter_data, { x: "sleep_hours", y: "reaction_time_ms", fill: "#457b9d", r: 5, fillOpacity: 0.75,
                       tip: true, title: d => `${d.sleep_hours}h sleep, ${d.reaction_time_ms}ms` }),
    ]
  })
}
```
:::
:::

::: {.fragment data-fragment-index="1"}
Same data, side by side. The lapse trials are still there — logging doesn't delete them — but on the raw scale they dominate the axis; logged, they no longer do, and the downward trend is much easier to see. Logging a skewed variable is a tool, not a rule: it helps here only because it actually makes the pattern clearer, and the online session goes further into why.
:::

## Covariance

In plain language: **covariance** asks whether x and y tend to move together — when one is above its own average, is the other usually above its average too?

::: {.fragment}
$$Cov[x,y] = \frac{\sum_i (x_i - \bar{x})(y_i - \bar{y})}{n}$$

- Multiplies each observation's deviation from the x-mean by its deviation from the y-mean, and averages
- Positive when x and y tend to deviate from their means **in the same direction**
- Can be any positive or negative number — units depend on the units of x and y
:::

::: {style="font-size:0.75em;color:#999;margin-top:12px;"}
Source: Békés & Kézdi (2021), Ch. 4
:::

## Task — calculate the covariance

::: {.instructions-box}
By hand or in Excel, using the class's (finger length, mean reaction time) pairs: calculate $Cov[\text{finger length}, \text{reaction time}]$.
:::

::: {.fragment}
```{ojs}
{
  const rows = student_summary.filter(d => d.finger_mm != null && !isNaN(d.finger_mm))
  if (rows.length < 3) return html`<p style="color:#aaa;">Will compute automatically once enough data is in.</p>`
  const xs = rows.map(d => d.finger_mm), ys = rows.map(d => d.mean_rt)
  const mx = d3.mean(xs), my = d3.mean(ys)
  const cov = d3.mean(xs.map((x,i) => (x - mx) * (ys[i] - my)))
  return html`<p style="font-family:sans-serif;">Cov[finger length, reaction time] = <strong style="color:#e63946;font-size:1.2em;">${cov.toFixed(1)}</strong></p>`
}
```
:::

## Correlation

In plain language: **correlation** asks the same question as covariance — do x and y move together — but reports the answer on a fixed scale from −1 to 1, so it's comparable no matter what units x and y are measured in.

The standardised version of the covariance — divide by the product of the standard deviations:

$$Corr[x,y] = \frac{Cov[x,y]}{SD[x] \, SD[y]} \qquad -1 \leq Corr[x,y] \leq 1$$

Rough guide: below 0.2 is weak, above 0.7 is generally strong.

## Task — calculate the correlation

::: {.instructions-box}
Using your covariance from two slides ago, and the SD of each variable: calculate the correlation coefficient.
:::

::: {.fragment}
```{ojs}
{
  const rows = student_summary.filter(d => d.finger_mm != null && !isNaN(d.finger_mm))
  if (rows.length < 3) return html`<p style="color:#aaa;">Will compute automatically once enough data is in.</p>`
  const xs = rows.map(d => d.finger_mm), ys = rows.map(d => d.mean_rt)
  const mx = d3.mean(xs), my = d3.mean(ys)
  const cov = d3.mean(xs.map((x,i) => (x - mx) * (ys[i] - my)))
  const corr = cov / (d3.deviation(xs) * d3.deviation(ys))
  return html`<p style="font-family:sans-serif;">Corr[finger length, reaction time] = <strong style="color:#e63946;font-size:1.2em;">${corr.toFixed(2)}</strong></p>`
}
```
:::

::: {.fragment}
Whatever number comes back — is it strong enough, on its own, to justify HR replacing the real test with a ruler?
:::

## Is it causal?

---

## Where does the variation in x come from?

Comparison requires **variation** in the conditioning variable — and where that variation comes from matters enormously.

::: {.two-col}
::: {.col}
**Experimental data**

- A treatment is assigned, often randomly
- Differences in y are attributable to the treatment alone
- e.g. randomly assign aspirin vs. placebo
:::
::: {.col}
**Observational data**

- x varies because of people's own choices, circumstances, history
- Many other things may differ alongside x
- e.g. people who already take aspirin routinely may do so *because* of prior health risk
:::
:::

::: {.fragment}
Almost everything in business analytics is observational. Finger length is one of the few genuinely fixed, "as-if-random" variables we're likely to find — most x's we'll meet from here on are not.
:::

::: {style="font-size:0.75em;color:#999;margin-top:12px;"}
Source: Békés & Kézdi (2021), Ch. 4
:::

## Task — find a spurious correlation

::: {.instructions-box}
Go to **tylervigen.com/spurious-correlations**. Find one example. In one sentence, explain why the two variables move together despite having no plausible causal link.
:::

::: {.fragment}
Correlation, on its own, never tells you which of these is true: **x causes y**, **y causes x**, **both are caused by something else**, or **coincidence**.
:::

---

## Measuring what you can't observe directly

---

## Latent variables

Some concepts — attitude, ability, management quality — can't be measured with a single variable. They're **latent**: real, but only indirectly observable through several proxies at once.

- **Use one variable** — simple, but throws away information
- **Average several (as z-scores)** — standardise first, then average; simple and transparent
- **PCA** — weights each variable by how well it captures the shared pattern; typically close to the simple average in practice

::: {style="font-size:0.75em;color:#999;margin-top:12px;"}
Source: Békés & Kézdi (2021), Ch. 4
:::

## Use one variable

The simplest approach: pick a single observable variable and treat it as a stand-in for the thing you can't measure directly.

- **Postcode** as a proxy for socioeconomic background
- **Job tenure** as a proxy for "experience"
- **Finger length** as a proxy for manual dexterity — this module's own opening example

::: {.fragment}
It's simple, and sometimes good enough. But a single proxy only ever captures **part** of the underlying concept — whatever it misses is thrown away, and if the proxy is a weak one, most of the concept goes with it.
:::

::: {.fragment}
::: {.instructions-box}
**Task** — our own reaction times aren't purely mechanical. What latent variables might actually be driving them — alertness, familiarity with the device, motivation on the day? What proxies do we already have sitting in our own data for any of these?
:::
:::

## Average several (as z-scores) {.smaller}

Suppose we want one "alertness" score for six people, from three imperfect proxies: hours of sleep, self-rated energy (1–10), and grip strength (kg).

```{ojs}
{
  const people = [
    { name: "Amara", sleep: 8.5, energy: 9, grip: 33 },
    { name: "Ben",    sleep: 5.0, energy: 4, grip: 32 },
    { name: "Chidi",  sleep: 7.0, energy: 6, grip: 35 },
    { name: "Dana",   sleep: 4.5, energy: 3, grip: 30 },
    { name: "Elin",   sleep: 9.0, energy: 8, grip: 31 },
    { name: "Femi",   sleep: 6.0, energy: 5, grip: 34 },
  ]
  return html`<table style="width:80%;margin:0 auto;border-collapse:collapse;font-family:sans-serif;font-size:0.85em;">
    <thead><tr style="background:#1a1a2e;color:white;">
      <th style="padding:7px 16px;text-align:left;">Person</th>
      <th style="padding:7px 16px;text-align:right;">Sleep (h)</th>
      <th style="padding:7px 16px;text-align:right;">Energy (1&ndash;10)</th>
      <th style="padding:7px 16px;text-align:right;">Grip (kg)</th>
    </tr></thead>
    <tbody>
      ${people.map((p,i) => `<tr style="${i%2===1?'background:#fafafa;':''}border-bottom:1px solid #eee;">
        <td style="padding:6px 16px;">${p.name}</td>
        <td style="padding:6px 16px;text-align:right;">${p.sleep}</td>
        <td style="padding:6px 16px;text-align:right;">${p.energy}</td>
        <td style="padding:6px 16px;text-align:right;">${p.grip}</td>
      </tr>`).join('')}
    </tbody>
  </table>`
}
```

::: {.fragment}
Different units, different scales — can't just add them. **Standardise each to a z-score first**, $z = (x - \bar{x}) / SD[x]$, then average the three z-scores per person.

```{ojs}
{
  const people = [
    { name: "Amara", sleep: 8.5, energy: 9, grip: 33 },
    { name: "Ben",    sleep: 5.0, energy: 4, grip: 32 },
    { name: "Chidi",  sleep: 7.0, energy: 6, grip: 35 },
    { name: "Dana",   sleep: 4.5, energy: 3, grip: 30 },
    { name: "Elin",   sleep: 9.0, energy: 8, grip: 31 },
    { name: "Femi",   sleep: 6.0, energy: 5, grip: 34 },
  ]
  const z = vals => { const m = d3.mean(vals), s = d3.deviation(vals) * Math.sqrt((vals.length-1)/vals.length); return vals.map(v => (v - m) / s) }
  const zs = z(people.map(p => p.sleep)), ze = z(people.map(p => p.energy)), zg = z(people.map(p => p.grip))
  const rows = people.map((p,i) => ({ name: p.name, zs: zs[i], ze: ze[i], zg: zg[i], avg: (zs[i]+ze[i]+zg[i])/3 }))

  return html`<table style="width:85%;margin:0 auto;border-collapse:collapse;font-family:sans-serif;font-size:0.85em;">
    <thead><tr style="background:#1a1a2e;color:white;">
      <th style="padding:7px 16px;text-align:left;">Person</th>
      <th style="padding:7px 16px;text-align:right;">z(sleep)</th>
      <th style="padding:7px 16px;text-align:right;">z(energy)</th>
      <th style="padding:7px 16px;text-align:right;">z(grip)</th>
      <th style="padding:7px 16px;text-align:right;background:#2d6a4f;">Average z</th>
    </tr></thead>
    <tbody>
      ${rows.map((r,i) => `<tr style="${i%2===1?'background:#fafafa;':''}border-bottom:1px solid #eee;">
        <td style="padding:6px 16px;">${r.name}</td>
        <td style="padding:6px 16px;text-align:right;">${r.zs.toFixed(2)}</td>
        <td style="padding:6px 16px;text-align:right;">${r.ze.toFixed(2)}</td>
        <td style="padding:6px 16px;text-align:right;">${r.zg.toFixed(2)}</td>
        <td style="padding:6px 16px;text-align:right;font-weight:700;background:#f0f4f8;color:#2d6a4f;">${r.avg.toFixed(2)}</td>
      </tr>`).join('')}
    </tbody>
  </table>`
}
```
:::

## PCA {.smaller}

Same six people, same three proxies. Instead of weighting every variable equally, **PCA looks at how the variables correlate with each other**, and finds the one weighted combination that captures as much of their *shared* variation as possible.

```{ojs}
{
  const rows = [
    { v: "Sleep",  sleep: 1.00, energy: 0.97, grip: 0.20 },
    { v: "Energy", sleep: 0.97, energy: 1.00, grip: 0.25 },
    { v: "Grip",   sleep: 0.20, energy: 0.25, grip: 1.00 },
  ]
  return html`<table style="width:60%;margin:0 auto;border-collapse:collapse;font-family:sans-serif;font-size:0.9em;">
    <thead><tr style="background:#1a1a2e;color:white;">
      <th style="padding:8px 16px;text-align:left;">Correlation</th>
      <th style="padding:8px 16px;text-align:right;">Sleep</th>
      <th style="padding:8px 16px;text-align:right;">Energy</th>
      <th style="padding:8px 16px;text-align:right;">Grip</th>
    </tr></thead>
    <tbody>
      ${rows.map((r,i) => `<tr style="${i%2===1?'background:#fafafa;':''}border-bottom:1px solid #eee;">
        <td style="padding:7px 16px;font-weight:700;">${r.v}</td>
        <td style="padding:7px 16px;text-align:right;">${r.sleep.toFixed(2)}</td>
        <td style="padding:7px 16px;text-align:right;">${r.energy.toFixed(2)}</td>
        <td style="padding:7px 16px;text-align:right;">${r.grip.toFixed(2)}</td>
      </tr>`).join('')}
    </tbody>
  </table>`
}
```

::: {.fragment}
Sleep and energy move together closely (0.97); grip strength barely tracks either (0.20–0.25) — a noisier signal for the same underlying "alertness."
:::

::: {.fragment}
PCA notices this automatically:

| Variable | Equal-weight average | PCA weight |
|---|---:|---:|
| Sleep | 0.33 | 0.41 |
| Energy | 0.33 | 0.41 |
| Grip | 0.33 | **0.18** |

It down-weights the noisier proxy — something a simple average, by construction, can't do.
:::

::: {.fragment}
The two composite scores still end up highly correlated (≈0.98 here) — usually true in practice. That's exactly why **Gabor & Kézdi recommend the z-score average for everyday use**, and treat PCA as a robustness check rather than a first choice.
:::

::: {style="font-size:0.75em;color:#999;margin-top:12px;"}
Source: Békés & Kézdi (2021), Ch. 4
:::

---

## AI and finding patterns

GenAI is genuinely useful for a first pass over a new dataset — spotting candidate patterns quickly, the way a quick script or profiler would.

::: {.fragment}
Where it's weaker: **judging** whether a correlation is meaningfully weak or strong, and knowing *which* pattern is worth pursuing in the first place. That judgment is still yours.
:::

::: {style="font-size:0.75em;color:#999;margin-top:12px;"}
Source: Békés & Kézdi (2021), Ch. 4
:::
